newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi TV facees legal cliffhanger.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi TV facees legal cliffhanger.

text.p: Former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi could face court action to take one of his television networks off the air next week because parliament has not met a deadline for new legislation, experts said on Sunday.
"From midnight on August 27 there will be a legal vacuum for the Italian television system," Francesco Casavola, head of a media watchdog body, told the Turin newspaper La Stampa.
A deadline for new anti-trust legislation governing television runs out at midnight on Tuesday August 27.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government approved a new broadcasting bill in July but it has not been passed into law. Parliament does not reconvene until after the deadline, which was set by the constitutional court.
The situation is particularly critical for media magnate Berlusconi, whose Mediaset broadcasting and advertising empire operates three television networks in Italy.
Mediaset was listed on the Milan stock exchange at the beginning of July and the company's stock price is sensitive to any legal threats to Berlusconi's broadcasting interests.

Casavola said that it was possible that one of Mediaset's three channels could be ordered off the air although he ruled out the possibility that all three networks -- Canale Cinque, Italia Uno and ReteQuattro -- could be shut down.

Italian newspapers speculated that any Italian magistrate could step in after August 27 and put one of the Mediaset channels in the dark because the legal void allowed different interpretations of current broadcasting legislation.
At present Italian broadcasting is regulated by the so-called Mammi law, named after Oscar Mammi, a telecommunications minister in the late 1980s.

The constitutional court ordered in December 1994 that a clause in the Mammi law allowing a single proprietor to operate three channels -- at the time 30 percent of the industry -- was unconstitutional and gave the government until August 27 of this year to come up with a new legal framework.
A magistrate could try to enforce the constitutional court ruling at any time after Tuesday on the grounds that the government had failed to enact new legislation.
The Prodi government's proposed bill, if passed into law, would force Mediaset to convert one of its three networks into a satellite or cable-television channel by August 1997.

Mediaset chairman Aldo Bonomo said that he believed the August 27 deadline was now irrelevent because the launch of new broadcasting channels by other operators in recent years had diluted Mediaset's share of broadcasting air time.
However, a close aide of Berlusconi, Gianni Letta, met prime minister Prodi on Friday and was reported to have appealed to the government to pass a decree law.
That would fill the imminent legal vacuum and allow parliament to give its seal of approval to the new legislation at a later date.
Prodi is believed to be reluctant to take such a step and Letta was expected to hold a further meeting with the prime minister on Monday.
